national_raw_news.content: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will address the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, today. The Summit is being held to mark the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. The SCO has ten member countries, including China and Russia. India has been a full member of the SCO since 2017. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his address to the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit, will underline India’s priorities in the areas of security, connectivity and opportunity. India has consistently opposed double standards in the fight against terrorism, separatism and extremism. India believes that greater connectivity among member countries is essential for peace and prosperity in the region. At the same time, connectivity projects must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries. India has also been emphasising the need to create new opportunities for the youth of member countries and promote the startup ecosystem. India believes that the energy, innovation and entrepreneurship of young people can give a fresh impetus to regional development and cooperation. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on the first day of his two-day visit to Kyrgyzstan yesterday, held bilateral meetings with the leaders of Russia, Iran, the Kyrgyz Republic and Armenia on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. The meetings covered various aspects of bilateral relations and issues of mutual interest. The Prime Minister also attended the official opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games in Bishkek yesterday evening, along with leaders of other SCO member countries. The biennial sporting event celebrates the rich sporting traditions, culture and heritage of nomadic civilisations.

national_raw_news.title: 45 mins ago | International 46 New Delhi rejects Court of Arbitration award on Indus Water Treaty
national_raw_news.content: India has strongly rejected a ruling by the World Bank-constituted Court of Arbitration over the Indus Waters Treaty, rejecting the tribunal’s authority and calling its decisions legally invalid. In a social media post, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said India has never recognised the arbitration panel, did not participate in its proceedings and would not be bound by its rulings. New Delhi also reiterated that the Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance. The statement came after the Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that India’s reasons for putting the treaty on hold did not justify its suspension or termination. The panel called on India to continue observing its obligations under the 1960 water-sharing agreement. India, however, rejected the ruling, arguing that the arbitration panel itself was established in violation of the terms of the treaty. The MEA said the panel has no jurisdiction whatsoever over India’s sovereign decisions concerning the treaty or its infrastructure projects. New Delhi suspended the Indus Waters Treaty following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year, citing national security concerns and continued cross-border terrorism. India has maintained that its decision on the treaty is a sovereign matter and that statements or rulings by the arbitration panel will not affect its actions related to water and infrastructure projects.

national_raw_news.title: 54 mins ago | International 28 Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers
national_raw_news.content: Rescue teams in Nepal are racing against time to reach more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in mud-filled tunnels at the Trishuli-3A hydropower site. Crews are using explosives, heavy machinery and air pumps to clear the tunnels and search for survivors. According to Nepal’s disaster management authority, 939 people have died, and 3,925 are missing, including 592 foreign nationals. So far, 279 people have been rescued from hydropower sites, while more than 11,000 people have been rescued across the country. The rescue operation is being supported by Nepalese and Chinese military teams, along with experts from India, South Korea and Australia. Severe flooding and landslides have made it difficult for rescuers to locate the buried tunnels. India has sent specialised teams to help with both rescue operations and the identification of victims. A 19-member Indian forensic team began work in Kathmandu, assisting with DNA testing to identify recovered remains. An Indian tunnel-rescue team is also working at hydropower sites in Chilime and Langtang. Experts are helping Nepalese authorities search for 933 workers and employees who have been missing since August 26, with many believed to be trapped inside the tunnels. At least 11 hydropower projects were damaged by the floods. Families say rescue efforts have been too slow and are urging authorities to act quickly. Downstream in Chitwan, nearly 300 bodies have been recovered from rivers. Many remain unidentified, so authorities are using DNA testing. Due to a shortage of freezers, some bodies have been temporarily buried until they can be identified. Nepal has asked several countries for help, including freezers, DNA-testing equipment, drones, bridges and specialised tunnel-rescue tools. A team of 18 Indian forensic experts is assisting with DNA identification. In Tibet, Chinese state media reports 16 deaths and 546 missing people. China has rejected claims that its hydropower projects caused the disaster, calling such allegations malicious speculation. The floods, believed to have been triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, have caused widespread destruction, damaging homes, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure across Nepal.
